script.opening: (Son, father present) "Honestly we think Dad’s just got dementia like Mum did — he’s forgetful and slow. But what’s really changed is his walking: he’s gone really unsteady, shuffling like his feet are stuck to the floor, and he’s had a couple of falls. And now — it’s upsetting — he’s started wetting himself. The family keep saying it’s just old age. Is there any point even looking into it?"

facts.text: Two role-players, or one playing both: the son, Gary (48, lives 10 minutes away, visits daily), and his father Harold (76), sitting beside him. Harold is happy for Gary to speak but answers when spoken to directly.

Started about 8–9 months ago: slower, small shuffling steps, "like his feet are glued to the floor", especially starting off and turning. Two falls in 3 months — tripped at the kitchen door, no head injury, didn’t black out. Harold: "My feet don’t want to go. I have to think about every step." On video, if asked, Gary can get Dad to walk across the room: short, wide-based shuffling steps, turning in several small steps.

Came after the walking, over the last 4–5 months: slower thinking, forgets appointments, repeats questions, "takes ages to answer". Still knows everyone, manages his own money with help, no getting lost. No hallucinations. Mood "a bit flat".
Last 3 months. Harold: "I get the urge and just don’t get there in time." Day and night. No burning, no blood. Not dribbling all the time. Bowels normal. Gary has bought pads.

Changes have been gradual — no sudden change, no confusion that comes and goes, no headaches, no fits. No tremor at rest that Gary has seen. No recent infection. Not drinking alcohol to excess (the odd sherry).

High blood pressure (amlodipine 5 mg), tamsulosin for "prostate" for 2 years, and his GP started oxybutynin 2 months ago "for the wetting" (if asked — it has made no difference, and Gary thinks he’s been "foggier" since). No sleeping tablets. No diabetes, no strokes known. No allergies.

Widower; wife died 3 years ago with Alzheimer’s, which Gary nursed her through. Harold lives alone in a two-storey house; bathroom upstairs. Ex-postman. Stopped driving last year. Gary is exhausted: works full time and has two teenagers.

Gary: loving but worn out and resigned, expects to be told nothing can be done; becomes hopeful but cautious if the doctor explains a treatable cause, and asks "So it might not be dementia at all?" Harold: quiet, embarrassed about the wetting, does not want to be a nuisance; responds warmly if the doctor speaks to him directly. Ask "An operation? At my age?" if a shunt is mentioned.

ice.ideas: Gary: "It’s dementia, like Mum. And old age." Harold: "I’m just getting old."
ice.concerns: Gary: "That he’ll fall and break his hip, and the wetting — it’s undignified for him." HIDDEN AGENDA — Gary watched his mum decline and assumes the same path; he is exhausted and half expecting to be told it’s time for a care home. Harold fears being "put in a home".
ice.expectations: Gary: "Honestly, I thought you’d say there’s nothing to be done." Hopes for some help with the falls and pads.

cues: "What’s really changed is his walking" — walking came first, the NPH pattern.
"Is there any point even looking into it?" — the family’s fatalism to address.
(Harold) "I don’t want to be a nuisance" — include and speak to the patient himself.

checkpoints.text: Recognises the NORMAL-PRESSURE HYDROCEPHALUS triad (gait disturbance + cognitive impairment + urinary incontinence, without informal mnemonics in front of the family) as a POTENTIALLY REVERSIBLE cause — not accepting "just dementia/old age"
Recognises that the GAIT disturbance (broad-based, shuffling, "magnetic", falls) is typically the EARLIEST/most prominent feature and a key pointer to NPH over Alzheimer’s/ageing

Still performs a REVERSIBLE-CAUSE work-up — medication review, bloods (B12/folate, TFTs, calcium, glucose, U&E, FBC), depression, Parkinson’s/parkinsonism, cerebrovascular disease, delirium/UTI, prostatic overflow/retention (NICE CG97), subdural haematoma after falls — with a face-to-face cognitive assessment, lying and standing BP and neurological/continence examination (not possible on video) — alongside considering NPH (NICE NG97)
Refers for NEUROLOGY/specialist assessment and BRAIN IMAGING (CT/MRI — ventricular enlargement out of proportion to atrophy), knowing CSF shunting can improve selected patients (gait responds best)
Arranges interim FALLS (NICE NG249 multifactorial assessment) and CONTINENCE support and addresses safety, while investigation/referral proceeds

Counters the family’s "just old age / is there any point" NIHILISM with the possibility of a reversible cause, while managing expectations realistically (not all NPH improves; coexisting pathology possible)

Supports the distressed SON/CARER, engages the PATIENT with dignity (not only the son), asking his permission before discussing him with his son and presuming capacity (Mental Capacity Act 2005), and checks understanding

Safety-nets and follows up: referral for imaging/specialist assessment, reversible-cause results, falls/continence support, carer support, and review — recognising and investigating a potentially reversible triad, not accepting "just dementia"

worked.txt: "I’m really glad you brought him, and I want to gently challenge the ‘just old age’ idea. The particular combination — the walking going first and badly, plus the memory AND the wetting — can be a specific condition called normal-pressure hydrocephalus, which, unlike most dementias, can sometimes be IMPROVED with treatment."

"What makes me think of it is that his WALKING is the standout problem — shuffling, feet stuck to the floor, falls — often more than the memory. In ordinary dementia the memory usually leads; here the gait does. That’s worth investigating, not dismissing."

"I’ll also do a proper check for other treatable things — review his medications, blood tests for vitamin levels, thyroid and calcium, screen for depression and a water infection, check his prostate isn’t stopping his bladder emptying, and make sure the falls haven’t caused a bleed on the brain, which can all cause similar problems. I’ll need to see him in person, or at home, to examine him properly, check his blood pressure lying and standing, and do a memory test."

"The key next step is a brain scan and a specialist assessment — in this condition the scan shows a particular pattern, and selected people benefit from a small procedure to drain the fluid, which can improve the walking especially. I’ll refer him."

"I want to be honest — not everyone improves, and there can be more than one thing going on. But it would be wrong not to look, because there’s a real chance of helping. ‘Is there any point?’ — yes, there genuinely is."

(To Mr Friske and son) "Meanwhile let’s get falls support and help with the continence — that’s important for dignity and safety. How are you managing as a family? I’ll arrange the referral and tests and review you. Come back sooner if he falls badly or becomes suddenly more confused."

f.learning: The combination of GAIT disturbance + COGNITIVE impairment + URINARY incontinence — the classic triad of NORMAL-PRESSURE HYDROCEPHALUS (NPH) (best not described to families with informal mnemonics) — is a POTENTIALLY REVERSIBLE cause of a dementia-like syndrome that must NOT be dismissed as "just dementia/old age", because CSF diversion (shunting) can improve symptoms (especially gait) in selected patients, and missing it loses a reversible opportunity. Crucially, the GAIT disturbance is typically the EARLIEST and most prominent feature — a broad-based, shuffling, slow, "magnetic"/feet-stuck gait with unsteadiness and falls — so a gait-led decline accompanied by incontinence and cognitive change should raise NPH rather than be attributed to Alzheimer’s or ageing. Still perform a thorough REVERSIBLE-CAUSE work-up for the same picture: medication review (sedatives/anticholinergics), bloods (NICE NG97: FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c/glucose, LFTs, TFTs, B12/folate), depression (pseudodementia), Parkinson’s/parkinsonism, cerebrovascular disease, and delirium (e.g. UTI causing confusion/incontinence), prostatic overflow or chronic retention (NICE CG97) and a subdural haematoma after falls, with a face-to-face cognitive assessment, lying and standing blood pressure and examination, as video cannot provide these (NICE NG97, NICE NG249). Refer for NEUROLOGY/specialist assessment and BRAIN IMAGING (CT/MRI showing ventricular enlargement out of proportion to cortical atrophy), with specialist assessment (including CSF tap-test response) determining shunt suitability. Support the distressed family/carer — counter the "just old age / is there any point?" nihilism with the possibility of a reversible cause while managing expectations realistically (not all NPH improves; coexisting pathology is possible), arrange interim falls and continence support, address carer needs, and engage the patient with dignity rather than only the relative, asking his permission before discussing him with his son (Mental Capacity Act 2005) and offering the son a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014). The hidden agenda is therapeutic nihilism; recognise the triad, investigate, refer, and support — not accept "just dementia".

knowledge.guideline: [1] NICE NG97 (dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, 2018) · [2] NICE NG249 (falls: assessment and prevention in older people and in people 50 and over at higher risk, 2025) · [3] NICE CG97 (lower urinary tract symptoms in men, 2010, updated 2015) · [4] NICE NG150 (supporting adult carers, 2020) · [5] Japanese Society of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus, guidelines for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, 3rd edition (2021) (international) · [6] Mental Capacity Act 2005 · [7] Care Act 2014
knowledge.summary: A 76-year-old whose walking went first — shuffling, feet ‘stuck to the floor’, falls — followed by slowed thinking and urinary incontinence has the classic triad of normal-pressure hydrocephalus. It is uncommon but potentially treatable, so ‘just dementia’ must not be accepted. Do the usual reversible-cause work-up, see him face to face, refer for imaging and specialist assessment, and support the family while this happens.

points.t: Gait disturbance, cognitive impairment and urinary urgency or incontinence. Gait usually comes first and dominates: slow, short steps, wide base, feet that seem stuck to the floor, poor turning and falls [5]. When walking leads the story, think beyond Alzheimer’s disease.

Selected patients improve after CSF shunting, with gait responding best and cognition least. Suitability is decided by specialists, often after a CSF tap test [5]. Not all improve, and other pathology often coexists — say so honestly.

NICE NG97 [1]: take a history from the person and someone who knows them; review medicines that may impair cognition (anticholinergic burden, sedatives); bloods — FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c, LFTs, TFTs, B12 and folate; urine testing if delirium is possible. Screen for depression and for delirium from infection.

NICE NG97 [1]: offer structural imaging to rule out reversible causes of cognitive decline and to help with subtype diagnosis. In normal-pressure hydrocephalus it shows ventricular enlargement out of proportion to atrophy [5]. Route per local pathway — neurology or the memory service.

NICE NG249 [2]: ask about falls; offer a comprehensive multifactorial assessment when criteria are met (for example injury, frailty or being unable to get up); use gait, balance and mobility tests rather than prediction tools; review medicines; offer strength and balance work.

NICE CG97 [3]: assess lower urinary tract symptoms — urine dipstick, frequency-volume chart, examination including abdomen and prostate, and check for retention. Overflow from prostatic enlargement and UTI are common mimics of ‘NPH incontinence’. Refer to the continence service for containment products meanwhile.

Speak to Mr Friske directly and ask his permission before discussing him with his son; presume capacity unless assessment shows otherwise (Mental Capacity Act 2005 [6]). Offer the son a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014 [7]) and information and support (NICE NG150 [4]).

On video you can watch him walk and talk, but a neurological examination, lying and standing blood pressure, a cognitive assessment and a continence examination need a face-to-face appointment or home visit.

Idea: just dementia or old age. Concern: falls, loss of dignity. Expectation: nothing can be done.
Warm, non-judgmental tone; put the patient at ease and showed respect for their perspective.
Opened broadly and let the patient tell their story before narrowing down.
When a cue was offered, stopped and explored the specific concern rather than reassuring superficially and moving on.
Active listening throughout — reflecting, pausing, not interrupting — interested in the patient as a person.
Told the patient why a question, examination or test was being done — transparent reasoning throughout.
Explained the working diagnosis or analysis in plain language the patient could understand.

ro.d: Addressed the patient’s specific concern — Gary: "That he’ll fall and break his hip, and the wetting — it’s undignified for him." HIDDEN AGENDA — Gary watched his mum decline and assumes the same path; he is exhausted and half expecting to be told it’s time for a care home. Harold fears being "put in a home" — directly within the plan, rather than noting it and moving on.
Checked understanding, offered written/follow-up support, asked if anything else was on their mind, agreed next steps.
Clear agenda set early, logical flow from data gathering to management. Did not jump to a plan before gathering enough information.
Explained clinical terms in plain English, or defined them immediately; checked the patient was following.
Noticed and responded to emotional and verbal cues rather than continuing a fixed clinical script.

model.text: Hello, I’m Dr Patel. Can I check who I’m speaking to? … Mr Friske, it’s good to see you — are you happy for your son to be with you and to talk about your health today?
model.why: Addresses the patient first and seeks his consent for the son to share

model.text: (Mr Friske) Yes, that’s fine.

(Son) Honestly, we think Dad’s just got dementia like Mum did — he’s forgetful and slow. But what’s really changed is his walking: he’s gone really unsteady, shuffling like his feet are stuck to the floor, and he’s had a couple of falls. And now — it’s upsetting — he’s started wetting himself. The family keep saying it’s just old age. Is there any point even looking into it?
Thank you both. There is a point, and I’ll explain why. First, can I ask some questions — Mr Friske, some to you and some to your son?
model.why: Answers the headline question briefly and sets an inclusive agenda

model.text: Mr Friske, how do you find your walking?
(Mr Friske) My feet don’t want to go. I have to think about every step.
(to son) Which came first — the walking, the memory, or the wetting? And over how long?
model.why: Establishes that gait led, and the time course over months

model.text: (Son) The walking, definitely. Over months. The memory and the accidents came after.

Could you both stand up and let me watch Mr Friske walk across the room and turn, if it’s safe with someone beside him? … Thank you. Those are short, slow steps with his feet close to the floor, and turning looks hard.
model.why: Uses video to observe gait safely; describes what is seen without over-claiming

model.text: Has anything changed suddenly — a sudden turn for the worse, being very muddled one day and better the next, a fever or burning when passing water? Did he hit his head in the falls? Any tremor?
model.why: Screens for delirium, UTI, subdural haematoma after falls and parkinsonism

model.text: (Son) No, it’s been gradual. No tremor that I’ve seen.
With the waterworks, does it come on as a sudden rush that he can’t hold, or is he dribbling all the time? Is he passing water often or feeling he hasn’t emptied?
model.why: Distinguishes urgency from overflow or retention

model.text: (Mr Friske) Hard to say. I just don’t get there in time.
(to son) You asked if there’s any point. What worries you most at the moment?
model.why: Explores the fatalism and the carer’s worry

model.text: (Son) That he’ll fall and break something. And the wetting — it’s undignified for him. We just assumed nothing could be done.
Mr Friske, how do you feel about all this?
model.why: Keeps the patient at the centre

model.text: (Mr Friske) Fed up. I don’t want to be a nuisance.

You’re not a nuisance at all. Here’s why this is worth looking into. The combination you describe — the walking going first and badly, then the memory, then the bladder — can be caused by a build-up of fluid in the brain called normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Unlike most types of dementia, it can sometimes be improved, especially the walking.
model.why: Names the NPH triad as potentially treatable and challenges ‘just dementia’

model.text: (Son) So it might not be dementia at all?
It might not, or there might be more than one thing going on. I want to be honest: not everyone with this improves. But it would be wrong not to look, when there’s a real chance of helping.

So, the plan. I’d like to see you in person, Mr Friske — at the surgery or at home — to examine your nerves and balance, check your blood pressure lying and standing, test your urine, check your bladder is emptying and your prostate, and do some memory questions. I’ll also go through your medicines, as some can affect memory and balance.
model.why: Face-to-face examination, continence assessment and medication review

model.text: (Son) We can do that.

I’ll arrange blood tests for vitamins, thyroid, calcium, kidneys and sugar, which can cause similar problems. And I’ll refer you for a brain scan and a specialist opinion. If it is this condition, the specialist may test whether draining a little fluid helps, and some people then have a small operation to drain it permanently.
model.why: NG97 reversible-cause bloods, imaging and specialist referral

model.text: (Mr Friske) An operation? At my age?

It would be your decision, with the specialist, and only if tests suggest it would help. Nothing is decided today. Meanwhile, I’ll refer you to the falls team for balance work and home safety, and to the continence service for practical help. (to son) And how are you and the family coping? You can have a carer’s assessment from the council, which can bring more support.
model.why: Interim falls and continence support, patient autonomy, carer’s assessment

model.text: (Son) That would help. It’s been a lot.

If he has a fall with a head injury, especially if he becomes drowsy, has a headache or is sick, or if he becomes suddenly much more confused, call 111 or 999 the same day. Could one of you tell me the plan?
model.why: Specific safety net for head injury and acute confusion; teach-back

model.text: (Son) You see Dad in person, bloods, a brain scan and specialist, falls team, continence help, carer’s assessment. Call if he falls and hits his head or gets suddenly worse.
That’s it exactly. I’ll book the visit this week and review everything once the results are in. Thank you for bringing him — you were right to ask.

social.t: Incontinence is often the hardest symptom for families and the reason care arrangements break down. Practical help from the continence service improves dignity quickly.
The family’s earlier experience of dementia (‘like Mum did’) may shape their fatalism. Acknowledge it without assuming the same diagnosis.

legal.t: Presume capacity; involve him in every decision, including any referral or future surgery. Assess capacity for a specific decision only if there is doubt. Suggest he considers lasting power of attorney while he can.
His son is entitled to a carer’s assessment from the local authority; Mr Friske may be entitled to a needs assessment.

professional.t: Seek his agreement before discussing him with his son (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Talk to him, not about him.
If he drives, a condition affecting cognition or mobility may need DVLA notification (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive). Ask at the face-to-face review.

community.t: Community falls service, continence service, local authority adult social care, Carers UK, and Hydrocephalus charity information (Shine) for patients and families.

redFlags: Fall with head injury, then drowsiness, headache or vomiting — possible subdural: same-day assessment
Sudden or fluctuating confusion — delirium (infection, drugs, retention)
Urinary retention or overflow; fever or dysuria
psychosocial: Family fatalism shaped by earlier experience of dementia (‘like Mum did’)
ice: Idea (family): just dementia or old age
Concern: falls and the distress of incontinence

playbook.diagnosis: Probable normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-led triad over months (magnetic, shuffling gait with falls; cognitive slowing; urinary incontinence) in a 76-year-old. Differential and contributors: Alzheimer’s or vascular dementia, parkinsonism, depression, delirium or UTI, overflow from prostatic enlargement, medicines, subdural haematoma after falls.
playbook.diagnosisLay: “Sometimes fluid builds up inside the brain and presses on the areas that control walking, the bladder and thinking. A scan can show it, and some people improve with treatment — especially their walking.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought nothing could be done. This pattern is worth looking into, because some of it may be treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Engage Mr Friske directly; respect his decisions; offer the son a carer’s assessment and support.
sharedPlan: Face-to-face review this week: neuro exam, gait, lying/standing BP, cognition, urine dip, bladder emptying, prostate, medication review
NICE NG97 bloods: FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c, LFTs, TFTs, B12 and folate
Brain imaging and specialist referral (neurology or memory service per local pathway)
Falls service (NICE NG249), continence service, carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014)
safetyNet: Fall with head injury then drowsiness, headache or vomiting, or sudden confusion — 111 or 999 the same day
Review after the visit and results

pitfalls.intro: This station tests whether you will challenge ‘just dementia’. The candidate who agrees with the family, or who talks only to the son, fails even with perfect knowledge.

items.fail: Accepting ‘just dementia’ and referring to the memory clinic without comment.
items.why: A gait-led triad suggests a potentially reversible cause.
items.fix: Name the triad, explain why it matters and request imaging with specialist review.

items.fail: Skipping the reversible-cause bloods and medication review once NPH is suspected.
items.why: NICE NG97 work-up still applies, and several causes may coexist.
items.fix: Order the NG97 bloods and review anticholinergics and sedatives.

items.fail: Assuming the incontinence is part of NPH.
items.why: Overflow from prostatic enlargement and UTI are common in older men.
items.fix: Urine dip, bladder emptying and prostate examination (NICE CG97).

items.fail: Talking about Mr Friske in the third person throughout.
items.why: It removes his dignity and ignores his capacity and consent.
items.fix: Address him first, ask his permission, ask his view.

items.fail: Promising that a shunt will fix it.
items.why: Not all improve and other pathology often coexists.
items.fix: Offer realistic hope: worth investigating, outcome uncertain.

items.fail: Claiming a neurological examination over video.
items.why: Remote findings are limited and examiners notice over-claiming.
items.fix: Observe gait on screen, then arrange a face-to-face review.

items.fail: No interim help for falls, continence or the carer.
items.why: Investigation takes weeks; harm happens meanwhile.
items.fix: Falls and continence referrals and a carer’s assessment now.

With the waterworks, does it come on as a sudden rush that he can’t hold, or is he dribbling all the time? Is he passing water often or feeling he hasn’t emptied?
SCA_MODELS.why: Distinguishes urgency from overflow or retention

SCA_MODELS.text: (Mr Friske) Hard to say. I just don’t get there in time.
(to son) You asked if there’s any point. What worries you most at the moment?
SCA_MODELS.why: Explores the fatalism and the carer’s worry

SCA_MODELS.text: (Son) That he’ll fall and break something. And the wetting — it’s undignified for him. We just assumed nothing could be done.
Mr Friske, how do you feel about all this?
SCA_MODELS.why: Keeps the patient at the centre

SCA_MODELS.text: (Mr Friske) Fed up. I don’t want to be a nuisance.

You’re not a nuisance at all. Here’s why this is worth looking into. The combination you describe — the walking going first and badly, then the memory, then the bladder — can be caused by a build-up of fluid in the brain called normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Unlike most types of dementia, it can sometimes be improved, especially the walking.
SCA_MODELS.why: Names the NPH triad as potentially treatable and challenges ‘just dementia’

SCA_MODELS.text: (Son) So it might not be dementia at all?
It might not, or there might be more than one thing going on. I want to be honest: not everyone with this improves. But it would be wrong not to look, when there’s a real chance of helping.

So, the plan. I’d like to see you in person, Mr Friske — at the surgery or at home — to examine your nerves and balance, check your blood pressure lying and standing, test your urine, check your bladder is emptying and your prostate, and do some memory questions. I’ll also go through your medicines, as some can affect memory and balance.
SCA_MODELS.why: Face-to-face examination, continence assessment and medication review

SCA_MODELS.text: (Son) We can do that.

I’ll arrange blood tests for vitamins, thyroid, calcium, kidneys and sugar, which can cause similar problems. And I’ll refer you for a brain scan and a specialist opinion. If it is this condition, the specialist may test whether draining a little fluid helps, and some people then have a small operation to drain it permanently.
SCA_MODELS.why: NG97 reversible-cause bloods, imaging and specialist referral

SCA_MODELS.text: (Mr Friske) An operation? At my age?

It would be your decision, with the specialist, and only if tests suggest it would help. Nothing is decided today. Meanwhile, I’ll refer you to the falls team for balance work and home safety, and to the continence service for practical help. (to son) And how are you and the family coping? You can have a carer’s assessment from the council, which can bring more support.
SCA_MODELS.why: Interim falls and continence support, patient autonomy, carer’s assessment

SCA_MODELS.text: (Son) That would help. It’s been a lot.

If he has a fall with a head injury, especially if he becomes drowsy, has a headache or is sick, or if he becomes suddenly much more confused, call 111 or 999 the same day. Could one of you tell me the plan?
SCA_MODELS.why: Specific safety net for head injury and acute confusion; teach-back

SCA_MODELS.text: (Son) You see Dad in person, bloods, a brain scan and specialist, falls team, continence help, carer’s assessment. Call if he falls and hits his head or gets suddenly worse.
That’s it exactly. I’ll book the visit this week and review everything once the results are in. Thank you for bringing him — you were right to ask.

SCA_STEM.name: Harold Friske
pmh: Falls — reported by family (not previously assessed)
meds: Check repeat list — review for sedatives and anticholinergics
SCA_STEM.recent: No recent bloods, cognitive assessment or imaging on file.
SCA_STEM.reason: Video consultation with his son. Months of unsteady shuffling walk with falls, forgetfulness and slowing, and new urinary incontinence. Family think it is ‘just dementia’.

SCA_KNOWLEDGE.guideline: [1] NICE NG97 (dementia: assessment, management and support for people living with dementia and their carers, 2018) · [2] NICE NG249 (falls: assessment and prevention in older people and in people 50 and over at higher risk, 2025) · [3] NICE CG97 (lower urinary tract symptoms in men, 2010, updated 2015) · [4] NICE NG150 (supporting adult carers, 2020) · [5] Japanese Society of Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus, guidelines for idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus, 3rd edition (2021) (international) · [6] Mental Capacity Act 2005 · [7] Care Act 2014
SCA_KNOWLEDGE.summary: A 76-year-old whose walking went first — shuffling, feet ‘stuck to the floor’, falls — followed by slowed thinking and urinary incontinence has the classic triad of normal-pressure hydrocephalus. It is uncommon but potentially treatable, so ‘just dementia’ must not be accepted. Do the usual reversible-cause work-up, see him face to face, refer for imaging and specialist assessment, and support the family while this happens.

points.t: Gait disturbance, cognitive impairment and urinary urgency or incontinence. Gait usually comes first and dominates: slow, short steps, wide base, feet that seem stuck to the floor, poor turning and falls [5]. When walking leads the story, think beyond Alzheimer’s disease.

Selected patients improve after CSF shunting, with gait responding best and cognition least. Suitability is decided by specialists, often after a CSF tap test [5]. Not all improve, and other pathology often coexists — say so honestly.

NICE NG97 [1]: take a history from the person and someone who knows them; review medicines that may impair cognition (anticholinergic burden, sedatives); bloods — FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c, LFTs, TFTs, B12 and folate; urine testing if delirium is possible. Screen for depression and for delirium from infection.

NICE NG97 [1]: offer structural imaging to rule out reversible causes of cognitive decline and to help with subtype diagnosis. In normal-pressure hydrocephalus it shows ventricular enlargement out of proportion to atrophy [5]. Route per local pathway — neurology or the memory service.

NICE NG249 [2]: ask about falls; offer a comprehensive multifactorial assessment when criteria are met (for example injury, frailty or being unable to get up); use gait, balance and mobility tests rather than prediction tools; review medicines; offer strength and balance work.

NICE CG97 [3]: assess lower urinary tract symptoms — urine dipstick, frequency-volume chart, examination including abdomen and prostate, and check for retention. Overflow from prostatic enlargement and UTI are common mimics of ‘NPH incontinence’. Refer to the continence service for containment products meanwhile.

Speak to Mr Friske directly and ask his permission before discussing him with his son; presume capacity unless assessment shows otherwise (Mental Capacity Act 2005 [6]). Offer the son a carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014 [7]) and information and support (NICE NG150 [4]).

On video you can watch him walk and talk, but a neurological examination, lying and standing blood pressure, a cognitive assessment and a continence examination need a face-to-face appointment or home visit.

SCA_SC_TASKS.d: Addressed Mr Friske first, gained consent for the son; let the son tell the story in full.
Explored falls impact, dignity, family fatalism and carer strain; kept Mr Friske in the conversation.
Picked up ‘the walking changed first’ and ‘is there any point?’ as the diagnostic and emotional cues.
Idea: just dementia or old age. Concern: falls, loss of dignity. Expectation: nothing can be done.
Observed gait on video; arranged face-to-face neuro, lying/standing BP, cognition, urine dip, bladder emptying, prostate; NG97 bloods.
NPH versus Alzheimer’s, vascular disease, parkinsonism, depression, delirium, UTI, overflow incontinence, subdural after falls.
Asked about sudden change, head injury in falls and infection; knew when same-day assessment was needed.
Probable NPH triad with gait-led onset; potentially reversible; coexisting pathology possible.
Brain imaging and specialist referral; medication review; falls service (NICE NG249); continence service; realistic shunt information.
Considered prostate, UTI and medicines as contributors; carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014).
Head injury and acute confusion safety net; face-to-face visit this week; results review; teach-back.

social.t: Incontinence is often the hardest symptom for families and the reason care arrangements break down. Practical help from the continence service improves dignity quickly.
The family’s earlier experience of dementia (‘like Mum did’) may shape their fatalism. Acknowledge it without assuming the same diagnosis.

legal.t: Presume capacity; involve him in every decision, including any referral or future surgery. Assess capacity for a specific decision only if there is doubt. Suggest he considers lasting power of attorney while he can.
His son is entitled to a carer’s assessment from the local authority; Mr Friske may be entitled to a needs assessment.

professional.t: Seek his agreement before discussing him with his son (GMC Confidentiality, 2017). Talk to him, not about him.
If he drives, a condition affecting cognition or mobility may need DVLA notification (DVLA Assessing fitness to drive). Ask at the face-to-face review.

community.t: Community falls service, continence service, local authority adult social care, Carers UK, and Hydrocephalus charity information (Shine) for patients and families.

redFlags: Fall with head injury, then drowsiness, headache or vomiting — possible subdural: same-day assessment
Sudden or fluctuating confusion — delirium (infection, drugs, retention)
Urinary retention or overflow; fever or dysuria
psychosocial: Family fatalism shaped by earlier experience of dementia (‘like Mum did’)
ice: Idea (family): just dementia or old age
Concern: falls and the distress of incontinence

SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosis: Probable normal-pressure hydrocephalus: gait-led triad over months (magnetic, shuffling gait with falls; cognitive slowing; urinary incontinence) in a 76-year-old. Differential and contributors: Alzheimer’s or vascular dementia, parkinsonism, depression, delirium or UTI, overflow from prostatic enlargement, medicines, subdural haematoma after falls.
SCA_PLAYBOOK.diagnosisLay: “Sometimes fluid builds up inside the brain and presses on the areas that control walking, the bladder and thinking. A scan can show it, and some people improve with treatment — especially their walking.”

management.reflectIce: “You thought nothing could be done. This pattern is worth looking into, because some of it may be treatable.”
management.psychosocial: Engage Mr Friske directly; respect his decisions; offer the son a carer’s assessment and support.

NICE NG97 bloods: FBC, ESR or CRP, U&E, calcium, HbA1c, LFTs, TFTs, B12 and folate
Brain imaging and specialist referral (neurology or memory service per local pathway)
Falls service (NICE NG249), continence service, carer’s assessment (Care Act 2014)
safetyNet: Fall with head injury then drowsiness, headache or vomiting, or sudden confusion — 111 or 999 the same day
Review after the visit and results

SCA_PITFALLS.intro: This station tests whether you will challenge ‘just dementia’. The candidate who agrees with the family, or who talks only to the son, fails even with perfect knowledge.

items.fail: Accepting ‘just dementia’ and referring to the memory clinic without comment.
items.why: A gait-led triad suggests a potentially reversible cause.
items.fix: Name the triad, explain why it matters and request imaging with specialist review.

items.fail: Skipping the reversible-cause bloods and medication review once NPH is suspected.
items.why: NICE NG97 work-up still applies, and several causes may coexist.
items.fix: Order the NG97 bloods and review anticholinergics and sedatives.

items.fail: Assuming the incontinence is part of NPH.
items.why: Overflow from prostatic enlargement and UTI are common in older men.
items.fix: Urine dip, bladder emptying and prostate examination (NICE CG97).

items.fail: Talking about Mr Friske in the third person throughout.
items.why: It removes his dignity and ignores his capacity and consent.
items.fix: Address him first, ask his permission, ask his view.

items.fail: Promising that a shunt will fix it.
items.why: Not all improve and other pathology often coexists.
items.fix: Offer realistic hope: worth investigating, outcome uncertain.

items.fail: Claiming a neurological examination over video.
items.why: Remote findings are limited and examiners notice over-claiming.
items.fix: Observe gait on screen, then arrange a face-to-face review.

items.fail: No interim help for falls, continence or the carer.
items.why: Investigation takes weeks; harm happens meanwhile.
items.fix: Falls and continence referrals and a carer’s assessment now.
